title: Metallurgy
tagline: From ore to metal: concentration, conversion, reduction — and the blast furnace that does all three at once.

overview.intro: Metallurgy answers one question: how do you get a metal out of rock and make it pure enough to use? The answer has three stages that never change — concentrate the ore, convert it to a form that reduction can attack, then reduce it to the metal. What changes between metals is which stage is difficult: iron is reduced with carbon in a blast furnace, aluminium needs electrolysis because carbon cannot touch it, and mercury is reduced by heating alone. Learn the three stages and the reasons for choosing one reagent over another, and every extraction question becomes a variation on the same story.

facts.label: Mineral vs ore
facts.value: An ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted profitably.

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: Removal of unwanted material from the ore, chosen by particle size, density or surface behaviour.

facts.label: Roasting and calcination
facts.value: Heating in air or without air to drive off volatile matter and form oxide.

facts.label: Reduction choice
facts.value: Carbon for iron, electrolysis for aluminium, heat alone for mercury.

learningOutcomes: Distinguish minerals from ores and describe the four concentration methods with the ore type each suits.
Explain roasting and calcination, stating the conditions and the products for each.
Compare the reduction of metal oxides by carbon, by hydrogen, by a more reactive metal and by electrolysis.
Describe the extraction of iron in the blast furnace, including the role of each reactant and the function of limestone.
Explain the extraction of aluminium and the protection of metals against corrosion, with alloy composition and use.

learn.title: Ores, gangue and concentrating the ore

blocks.text: Metals occur in the earth’s crust combined or free, and the compound forms we dig up are minerals. An ore is simply the mineral worth mining, because the metal can be extracted at a price someone will pay. The worthless material mixed with it is called gangue, usually sand and rocky silicates, and the first job of metallurgy is to remove it. The method chosen depends on the physical difference between ore and gangue: hand picking where particles are visible, washing where the ore is much denser than the sand, magnetic separation where one component is magnetic, and froth flotation where the ore is preferentially wetted by oil while the gangue is wetted by water. Froth flotation is the standard method for sulphide ores such as zinc blende and galena, and it is the one the examination names most often.

items: Hand picking is used when the ore particles can be seen and separated by eye, as with red haematite in brown earth.
Levigation or washing uses a stream of water to carry away lighter sand while the denser ore settles.
Magnetic separation suits an ore mixed with a non-magnetic impurity when one of the two is magnetic, as with haematite and tin stone.
Froth flotation uses an oil such as pine oil; sulphide particles attach to froth and are skimmed off.

items.note: Crushed ore is mixed with oil and water; lead sulphide froths up with the oil while sand sinks.
Magnetic wolframite is drawn to the magnet while non-magnetic tin stone passes on.

learn.title: Making the oxide: calcination and roasting

blocks.text: Very few metals are ever reduced straight from the raw ore; the intermediate step is almost always the oxide, because metal oxides are easier to reduce than sulphides or carbonates. Two heating treatments prepare that oxide. Calcination heats the ore strongly without air, which is what carbonates need: calcium carbonate and zinc carbonate split into oxide and carbon dioxide. Roasting heats the ore strongly with excess air, which is what sulphides need: zinc sulphide becomes zinc oxide and sulphur dioxide. Some ores need both, in sequence, and the choice follows directly from what the ore is made of. Both processes also drive off moisture and any volatile impurity, so the product is a cleaner, more reactive starting material for reduction.

items: Calcination: strong heating without air; used for carbonates, driving off carbon dioxide.
Roasting: strong heating in excess air; used for sulphides, forming oxide and sulphur dioxide.
Both stages remove moisture and volatile impurities from the concentrated ore.
The oxide produced is more readily reduced than the original sulphide or carbonate.

items.note: ZnCO3 on strong heating gives ZnO and CO2, with the solid losing weight as gas escapes.
2ZnS + 3O2 → 2ZnO + 2SO2; the sulphur dioxide is captured to make sulphuric acid.

items.meaning: Sandy or rocky impurity associated with an ore and removed in concentration.
Strong heating of an ore without air, usually to decompose a carbonate.
Strong heating of an ore in excess air, usually to convert a sulphide to an oxide.
Substance added to react with gangue and form a removable slag.

learn.title: Four ways to reduce a metal oxide

blocks.text: The reduction step supplies electrons back to the metal ion, and the cheapest reagent that can do the job wins. Carbon is the industrial favourite: it takes oxygen away at high temperature and is itself oxidised to carbon monoxide or carbon dioxide, which is how iron and zinc are made. Hydrogen can do the same job for metals such as copper and tungsten, leaving only water behind. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive one from its oxide, and this aluminothermic method is used when a very high temperature is needed locally, as in welding rails, because the reaction is violently exothermic. When the metal is too reactive for any of these — aluminium, sodium, calcium — only electrolysis of the molten oxide or chloride will do, since electricity is the only force strong enough to hand electrons back to such stable ions.

items: Carbon reduction suits metals below carbon in the activity series, notably iron and zinc.
Hydrogen reduction gives a clean product with water as the only by-product.
Aluminothermic reduction: metal oxide plus aluminium gives metal plus aluminium oxide and intense heat.
Electrolytic reduction is required for aluminium, sodium and calcium because their ions hold electrons very tightly.

items.note: Fe2O3 + 2Al → 2Fe + Al2O3 with enough heat to make molten iron, used to join rail tracks.
Heating with hydrogen gives reddish copper and steam, showing hydrogen as a reducing agent.

blocks.text: The blast furnace makes iron by running all three metallurgical stages at once in a single tall shaft. Down the top fall coke, limestone and concentrated haematite; up the bottom blast hot air. Near the base, coke burns to carbon dioxide and the heat raises the temperature to about 1900 °C. Higher up the carbon dioxide reacts with more coke to give carbon monoxide, which is the true reducing agent: it strips oxygen from haematite to give molten iron and carbon dioxide. Limestone decomposes to calcium oxide, which removes the acidic silica impurity as calcium silicate slag — a floating liquid that is tapped off separately because it is less dense than the molten iron. The two taps, one giving pig iron and one giving slag, are the physical proof that the furnace is doing three jobs at once.

items: Coke provides heat by burning and provides the reducing agent as carbon monoxide.
Limestone decomposes to calcium oxide, which combines with silica to form calcium silicate slag.
Haematite is reduced in stages, ending with molten iron that dissolves a little carbon.
Molten slag floats on molten iron because it is less dense, so the two are tapped at different levels.

items.note: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2, taking oxygen away from the iron ore at high temperature.
CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3, the slag that carries the acidic gangue out of the furnace.

blocks.caption: What happens at each level of the blast furnace

blocks.text: Aluminium cannot be reduced with carbon because aluminium oxide is far more stable than carbon dioxide, so the metal is made by electrolysis. Purified alumina dissolves in molten cryolite, which lowers the operating temperature and saves power, and a little fluorspar helps the mixture conduct. The cathode is the lining of the steel cell, the anode is a set of carbon rods, and oxygen evolved at the anode burns the rods away — a cost the industry accepts because the alternative reaction is impossible. Corrosion is the slow return of a metal to its oxide or sulphide form in air and moisture, and it is prevented by barrier methods such as painting, greasing and galvanising, or by sacrificial protection in which a more reactive metal corrodes instead. Alloys are deliberately mixed metals whose different-sized atoms disrupt the regular lattice, making it harder for layers to slide — which is why brass and stainless steel outperform either component alone.

items: Purified Al2O3 is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point and increase conductivity.
Carbon anodes burn to carbon dioxide as oxygen is liberated, so they need periodic replacement.
Galvanising coats iron with zinc, which protects even if the coating is scratched, because zinc corrodes preferentially.
Alloys are harder than pure metals because different atom sizes distort the layers and block slip.

items.note: Aluminium with copper, magnesium and manganese: light and strong, used in aircraft skin.
Iron with chromium and nickel; the chromium oxide film stops rust forming at the surface.

keyPoints: An ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably; the unwanted material is gangue.
Concentration methods: hand picking, levigation, magnetic separation and froth flotation, each matched to a physical difference.
Calcination heats without air and suits carbonates; roasting heats in air and suits sulphides.
Carbon reduces the oxides of iron and zinc; aluminium reduces refractory oxides in the thermite reaction.
Aluminium, sodium and calcium require electrolytic reduction because their ions are too stable for chemical reduction.
In the blast furnace coke burns for heat and forms the reducing gas carbon monoxide, while limestone removes silica as slag.
Slag floats on molten iron because it is less dense, so iron and slag are tapped separately.
Alumina is electrolysed in molten cryolite to cut the melting point and power cost.
Corrosion is prevented by barrier coatings or by sacrificial protection with a more reactive metal.
Alloys are harder than pure metals because atoms of different sizes distort the lattice and prevent layers from slipping.
examFocus: Name the method and the property it exploits: froth flotation for sulphides, magnetic separation for magnetic ores.
The blast furnace requires the reactions at each zone with temperature ranges — learn them as a top-to-bottom story.
Say why carbon cannot reduce alumina when asked about aluminium; the comparison with iron is the point of the question.
For corrosion, give both a barrier method and a sacrificial method with one named example each.

vocabulary.meaning: Mineral from which a metal can be extracted commercially.
Rocky or sandy impurity removed from an ore during concentration.
Liquid formed when flux reacts with gangue; it floats on the molten metal.
Substance added to combine with gangue and make it removable.
Heating an ore in air to convert a sulphide into an oxide.
Heating an ore without air to decompose a carbonate or drive off moisture.
Substance that removes oxygen from another, and is itself oxidised.
Mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, chosen to alter properties.

questions.prompt: The method used to concentrate sulphide ores is:
questions.explanation: Sulphide particles are preferentially wetted by oil and rise with the froth while gangue sinks.

questions.prompt: Calcination is the heating of an ore:
questions.explanation: Calcination excludes air so that carbonates can decompose to oxide and carbon dioxide without further oxidation.

questions.prompt: In the blast furnace, the reducing agent that actually removes oxygen from haematite is:
questions.explanation: Coke burns to carbon dioxide which then forms carbon monoxide, and the carbon monoxide performs the reduction.

questions.prompt: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than reduction with carbon because:
options: Aluminium oxide is more stable than carbon dioxide
questions.answer: Aluminium oxide is more stable than carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Carbon cannot take oxygen from alumina because alumina has a lower free energy of formation under those conditions.

questions.prompt: The worthless sandy material mixed with an ore is called __________.
questions.explanation: Gangue is removed first, by concentration, before any chemical treatment begins.

questions.prompt: A substance added to react with gangue so that it can be removed as slag is called a __________.
questions.explanation: Limestone is the common acidic-gangue flux because it decomposes to calcium oxide in the furnace.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a mineral and an ore.
questions.answer: A mineral is a naturally occurring solid chemical compound from which a metal may be extracted, while an ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted profitably by a practicable process.
questions.explanation: Every ore is a mineral, but a mineral becomes an ore only when extraction is economically viable.

questions.prompt: Explain why zinc blende is roasted before it is reduced.
questions.answer: Roasting converts the sulphide to oxide by heating it in air: 2ZnS + 3O2 → 2ZnO + 2SO2. The oxide is far easier to reduce with carbon than the sulphide would be, and the sulphur dioxide can be captured for sulphuric acid manufacture.
questions.explanation: The sulphur must leave as gas first, otherwise reduction with coke would be inefficient and polluting.

questions.prompt: State one method of protecting iron from corrosion and explain how it works.
questions.answer: Galvanising coats iron with zinc; even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes preferentially because it is more reactive than iron, so the iron underneath remains protected.
questions.explanation: Barrier protection stops air and water reaching the surface, while sacrificial protection uses a more reactive metal.

questions.prompt: Describe the extraction of iron in the blast furnace, giving the reactions at the top, middle and base and the role of limestone.
questions.answer: Coke, limestone and concentrated haematite are charged at the top while hot air is blasted at the base. Near the base, coke burns: C + O2 → CO2, releasing heat and raising the temperature to about 1900 °C. In the middle zone the carbon dioxide passes over hot coke and is reduced: CO2 + C → 2CO, so carbon monoxide rises through the charge. In the upper zone it reduces the ore: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2, and the molten iron trickles to the bottom. Limestone decomposes to calcium oxide, which combines with acidic silica to give calcium silicate slag; the less dense slag floats and is tapped separately, leaving fairly pure iron below.
questions.explanation: One furnace performs concentration-independent heating, oxide reduction and impurity removal simultaneously, at different heights.

questions.prompt: Compare the extraction of aluminium with that of iron, explaining why different methods are used.
questions.answer: Iron is reduced chemically in the blast furnace using carbon monoxide generated from coke, because iron oxide is sufficiently stable to be reduced by carbon at high temperature. Aluminium cannot be obtained this way because aluminium oxide is more stable than carbon dioxide, so carbon will not take its oxygen. Instead purified alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the operating temperature and is electrolysed with carbon electrodes, the cathode being the cell lining and the anode a set of carbon rods. Oxygen evolved at the anode burns the rods away, a cost that reflects the extreme stability of alumina.
questions.explanation: The choice of method follows the thermodynamic stability of the oxide relative to carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: An ore contains a light coloured sulphide mixed with sand and a small amount of magnetic impurity. Outline a scheme that would give a pure sample of the metal and justify each choice.
questions.answer: First concentrate by froth flotation, since the target is a sulphide: oil wets the sulphide particles and carries them into the froth while the sand sinks. If the magnetic impurity reports with the concentrate, a magnetic separation step can remove it before chemical treatment. Next roast the concentrate in air to convert the sulphide to oxide and drive off sulphur dioxide. Finally reduce the oxide with carbon if the metal sits below carbon in the activity series, or by electrolysis if it is more reactive, and purify the crude metal as required. Each stage exploits a different property — surface behaviour for flotation, magnetism for separation, chemical reactivity for reduction.
questions.explanation: A separation sequence must move from cheapest physical methods to the more expensive chemical ones, using the property that distinguishes each unwanted component.
